Russia-Ukraine War Germany Is Daily Target of Hybrid Warfare, Minister Says The remarks came days after a drone fitted with an explosive device was found at the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Police officers work in the vicinity of an Antonov cargo plane, near which a drone was found, at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Schkeuditz, Germany, on Aug. 5, 2026. Axel Schmidt/Reuters Victoria Friedman 8/10/2026 | Updated: 8/10/2026 0:00 X 1 Germany is facing daily hybrid warfare attacks from foreign adversaries, a senior minister has said, following a suspected attempted drone attack on the Leipzig/Halle Airport last week. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told BILD on Aug. 8 that he would not use the term “war” to describe the current situation but that he believed that “the palpable strategic goal of foreign powers is to subjugate [Germany] politically and socially.” “We are a daily target of hybrid warfare,” Dobrindt told the German newspaper. “Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or directly harming it are a constant reality.” Dobrindt did not identify a particular country. A hybrid attack falls short of an act of war and can include sabotage, propaganda, and other non-overt tactics. On Aug. 4, a drone fitted with an explosive device was found at the Leipzig/Halle Airport by staff, with German prosecutors saying that there was sufficient evidence to suggest that an explosion was intended to be caused by the craft. Related Stories Crimea Strikes Could Rise Sevenfold With Faster Western Funding: Ukrainian Drone Commander Drone Discovered at Airport Fitted With Explosive Device, Says German Prosecutor The Federal Prosecutor’s Office said on Aug. 6 that “this constitutes a serious attack on the transport and logistics infrastructure in Germany.” Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key cargo hub and military airport in the state of Saxony in eastern Germany. It is the main base for NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution. Among other functions, it delivers equipment to strengthen the ​defense pact’s eastern flank, ⁠using a small fleet of Ukrainian-made Antonov cargo planes. Dobrindt, at the time, described the incident as a “hybrid attack.” Authorities have not identified any suspects, but Dobrindt said he could not rule out “foreign powers.” In the past, German lawmakers have blamed Russia for hybrid attacks—accusations that Moscow has repeatedly denied. The Russian Embassy in Berlin on Aug. 7 dismissed the incident, denying that Moscow was involved in any hybrid attacks. The embassy said in a post on Telegram on Aug. 7 that the incident was a “hastily concocted provocation,” saying that it was another unsubstantiated accusation against Russia. Drones Spotted Over Military Base Days after the airport incident, German authorities said that two drones were spotted over a military base in the western part of the country. A spokesperson for the German armed forces, the Bundeswehr, said the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) were sighted at about 10 p.m. local time on Aug. 6 at the base in Mechernich in the state ​of North Rhine-Westphalia, some 22 miles from the ⁠border with Belgium. Drones have become a major feature of warfare in the Russia–Ukraine conflict, with UAVs from both sides causing damage to infrastructure and fuel supply lines. However, UAVs operating close to the European border had resulted in vehicles unintentionally straying into NATO territory. Late last month, Romanian officials said they had shot down three Russian drones in as many days, prompting Bucharest to expel the Russian ambassador, Vladimir Lipaev. Romania, a NATO member, shares a 400-mile land border with Ukraine, and Russian UAVs have repeatedly violated its airspace during the more than four-year war. Lipaev dismissed the alleged Russian violations of Romanian airspace, protesting what he said was an “unjustified expulsion” of an embassy employee. Ukrainian drones have also been downed in allied territory, although Kyiv has frequently blamed the incursions on electronic interference from Russian military forces. Reuters contributed to this report. https://www.dw.com/en/niger-s-defense-mi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JbU1 The main airport in Niamey was reportedly targeted by the attacks [FILE: August 8, 2026] Image: Sam Mednick/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Niger's Ministry of National Defense ‌on ⁠Saturday said ⁠that ​a group of soldiers shot at "sensitive" locations in the capital Niamey in an apparent mutiny. Gunfire and explosions had been heard across Niger's capital, Niamey, overnight into the early hours of Saturday morning. Attackers had targeted Diori Hamani International Airport, which also houses a military air base, and attempted to breach the security perimeter around ​the presidency. "Another cowardly attack on Base 101 and once again our defense and security forces ensured ... Situation under control," said lawmaker Bana Wagana Ibrahim, who serves on the Consultative Council. Niger military 'gradually regaining control' The military said it was "gradually regaining control" after mutineers took soldiers hostage at a base near the airport in Niamey, AFP news agency reported. Authorities urged the public to "remain calm and freely go about their business" in a statement read out on public television and signed by Defense Minister General Salifou Mody. The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani , who seized power in a 2023 coup. Niger, like its Sahelian neighbors Mali and Burkina Faso , has for years been ruled by a military junta that has struggled to stem a jihadi insurgency. National TV signal reportedly cut after gunfire The shooting began around 1 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) and continued until daybreak. Locals said that the country's national television had gone off air. Tele Sahel's satellite and online programming was replaced with a black screen at 9 a.m. local time (0800 GMT), AFP reported. It was restored around one hour later. Niamey has been targeted by jihadists twice this year: once by the so-called "Islamic State in the Sahel" group (EIS) and again in June by their rivals from the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM). https://www.mediafax.ro/english/nicusor-.text: Nicușor Dan’s Message Following the Death of King Harald V Romanian President Nicușor Dan issued a message of condolence on Friday following the death of King Harald V of Norway at the age of 89. The Romanian head of state extended his condolences to the new King Haakon, Queen Sonja, the royal family, and the Norwegian people. The message was posted by Nicușor Dan on Platform X shortly after the Norwegian monarch’s death was announced. Nicușor Dan: “I received the news with deep sadness” The President of Romania stated that he received the news of King Harald V’s death “with deep sadness.” “I extend my sincere condolences, including on behalf of the Romanian people, to His Majesty King Haakon, Queen Sonja, the entire royal family, and the people of Norway, and I share in their grief,” Nicușor Dan said. The Romanian head of state thus expressed his solidarity with the royal family and the Norwegian people during this time of mourning. Harald V died at the age of 89 King Harald V died on Friday at the age of 89. The monarch had been on the Norwegian throne since 1991 and reigned for 35 years. Following his death, the throne is assumed by his son, Haakon, to whom Nicușor Dan addressed a message using the title “His Majesty King Haakon.” Harald V was regarded as one of the figures who contributed to the modernization of the Norwegian monarchy and enjoyed high popularity among the population. In recent years, the king had scaled back his public activities due to health issues. Harald V leaves behind a reign that spanned more than three decades of political and social transformation in Norway. Queen Sonja, to whom he was married for nearly six decades, and the other members of the royal family were by the king’s side in the days leading up to his death. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.text: Image source, Christy Spivey By Sareen Habeshian Â and Â Brandon Drenon Published 25 September 2026 Updated 1 hour ago Warning: This story contains distressing details Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree. The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs. The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August. The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests. In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged". Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged. Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembers the coroner telling her: "we're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree. Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related". Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Spivey described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end. "I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added. Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail. "I just hope they have the right people," she said. Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond. A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week. A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday. The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country. Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress , external , which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers. The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide. Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters View image in fullscreen Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be livestreamed. Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters Capital punishment Analysis Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company Jason Burke Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice US politics – live updates Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.55 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 14.07 EDT Share If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years. Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International . In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed. In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows. View image in fullscreen Protesters gathered last year in Paris and other cities around the world to demand an end to executions in Iran. Photograph: Siavosh Hosseini/LightRocket/Getty Images Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities. Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror. Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority. Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones. In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook . View image in fullscreen The planned public execution of Nidal Hasan would be the first in the US in many decades. Photograph: Reuters The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades. In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City. Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December . Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did. 11:14 ‘Barbaric’ firing squad livestream ordered by Pete Hegseth - The Latest Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years. In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran , its highest number of executions in decades. Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”. “This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported. https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.text: Antisemitism envoy Jillian Segal says modern ‘progressive’ antisemitism is the most pervasive form of the prejudice in Australia. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Antisemitism envoy Jillian Segal says modern ‘progressive’ antisemitism is the most pervasive form of the prejudice in Australia. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images Australian media Antisemitism envoy proposes ‘external ombudsman’ to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of Israel and Middle East Jillian Segal says perception of link between coverage of conflicts and hostility towards Jewish Australians ‘is itself a matter of public importance’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Doherty Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.37 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 23.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The federal government’s antisemitism envoy has proposed an “external independent ombudsman” to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of the war in Gaza, and a requirement that all visa applicants be screened for “the risk of holding antisemitic views”. In an updated plan released on Friday , Jillian Segal said Australia’s two public broadcasters should be subjected to greater oversight. “Given the extent and seriousness of concerns about subjective, inaccurate and disproportionate reporting in accordance with its own standards, it would be in the public interest for the public broadcasters’ coverage and approach to be the subject of more detailed analysis and independent review,” Segal wrote in the new plan. Lawyers for Marist Brothers face questions over advice to keep serial offender out of ‘legal arena’ Read more It suggests that a government-appointed panel review the public broadcasters’ previous reporting and states the government should consider “transferring” responsibilities from the ABC and SBS ombudsmen to an “external independent ombudsman consistent with other sectors such as telecommunications and banking”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Segal writes that “Jewish Australians have reported being abused, harassed and accused of being ‘baby killers’ or supporters of ‘genocide’ simply for their belief in the right of Israel to exist”. “That perception of a link between coverage and hostility is itself a matter of public importance.” Segal said she had received “many expressions of concern from the Australian Jewish community” about ABC and SBS reporting on “Israel and the conflict in the Middle East”. The special envoy to combat antisemitism’s initial plan, released in mid-2025 , said Segal would “work with the publicly funded broadcasters to encourage them to develop programs that add to social cohesion”. She then told the royal commission into antisemitism in mid-2026 she wanted a new “oversight” committee that could give ABC and SBS coverage a “tick” or “guidance”. Segal told Senate estimates this week she was concerned about “the tone [and] the frequency of reporting about Gaza from the ABC”. The broadcasters rejected calls for external oversight last year. On Friday, the ABC said its complaints process was “the most robust and transparent in the Australian media”. “The ABC has the highest editorial standards and a comprehensive framework to ensure accountability, transparency and high editorial standards,” a spokesperson said. “This framework is designed to balance accountability with editorial independence and robust journalism.” The royal commission was established in response to the Bondi beach massacre in December when 15 people were killed during a Hanukah celebration. Visa applicants to to be screened Friday’s report proposes that all visa applicants wanting to travel to Australia should be assessed for “the risk of holding antisemitic views”. “It would be disingenuous not to acknowledge that a minority of migrants bring to Australia ingrained antisemitic views. This is often a function of migrating from countries or environments where antisemitism is commonplace and reinforced by political, religious, educational and cultural institutions or leadership,” Segal writes. The report states the home affairs department should prioritise “the identification of antisemitic conduct before visa grant, including through new technological capabilities and thorough consideration of information already recorded on a client’s record”. The arts and universities Segal suggests publicly funded arts organisations should be able to impose “enforceable conditions” on artists and terminate grants if they promoted antisemitism. The envoy states that all arts organisations – private and public – should develop policies to govern the use of their venues, festivals and stages or “artists’ personal political or ideological activism outside the scope of the advertised show, performance or exhibition”. The envoy’s updated plan proposes allowing grant authorities to impose enforceable conditions on academics, allowing “for the termination of grant funding … where the recipient engages in antisemitic speech or conduct”. Segal said the proposals outlined in the plan were “not about silencing criticism of Israel”. The report argues that “modern, progressive antisemitism” was the most pervasive form of the prejudice in Australia. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “It takes the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes, and gives it a respectable face through the language of social justice and human rights”. Segal said Islamic extremism, far-left and far-right antisemitism were prevalent “and they require vigilance and laws that are properly enforced”. “But the form that is leaving Jewish Australians increasingly anxious and excluded is the one that has taken root in influential institutions, where Jewish Australians are being discriminated against, blamed and vilified for the actions of the government of the state of Israel.” Comment was being sought from SBS, Universities Australia and the Australian Palestine Advocacy Network. ‘Trumpian’ The progressive Jewish Council of Australia on Friday criticised the envoy’s new plan as “Trumpian”, arguing it was a “dangerous and ideologically driven roadmap that threatens freedom of speech, academic freedom and democratic rights, while failing to meaningfully address the causes of antisemitism”. The council said the envoy’s claims about “progressive antisemitism” verged on “conspiratorial”. Bart Shteinman, an executive officer at the JCA, said Friday’s report did “little to mask a rightwing ideology that will go to incredible lengths to silence those drawing attention to Israel’s genocide in Gaza” and that it sought “unprecedented oversight” over media, the arts and other organisations. “What Segal is proposing as the path forwards to combatting antisemitism is similar to what we might expect coming out of Trump’s America, not Australia.” Shteinman urged the federal government to remember that “the special envoy does not speak for all Jews, many of whom could be classified as ‘progressive antisemites’ themselves under the ridiculous analysis Segal is promoting”. Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, told 2GB radio that Segal’s decision to highlight “far-left antisemitism” was “insightful and courageous”. “Antisemitism comes from different facets of society, but with the far left, it’s laced in this dishonesty. It’s packaged in the language of human rights, of compassion, and peace, and progressivism, but actually, they repurpose classic neo-Nazi antisemitic tropes.” Ryvchin said within the ABC and SBS “there is a certain culture, there is a certain groupthink, which I think is driven by almost a handful of journalists and executives, who have this kind of political ideology, which they then coach and mentor through the organisation”. He said genuine accountability could only be acheived “through external accountability”. The release of the envoy’s updated plan came two days after Segal appeared at Senate estimates. She defended previously criticising SBS for quoting death toll figures provided by the Gaza’s health ministry. She told the royal commission the figures were “grossly inflated” and their inflation was “well known and even accepted by the United Nations”. A spokesperson for the UN secretary general responded at the time: “For us [the UN], the Ministry of Health in Gaza is a source we, and many others, often cite. Independent validation of subsets of the data has found no significant discrepancies in their numbers.” Segal told the estimates hearing this week she accepted the UN view “but that does not detract from the concerns of the Jewish community as conveyed to me about the way in which the reporting had been done”. Israel’s military accepted in January that the death toll compiled by health authorities in Gaza was broadly accurate.
